sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hymir** (*hymir*) — Giant, Owner of Cauldron · the Dark One of Heaven's End — is the sea-giant of *Hymiskviða*: the fierce host east of the Élivágar whose hall stands on his herd of cattle, whose treasure is the mile-deep cauldron [[aegir|Ægir]] demands for the brewing of the gods' ale, and whose fishing-trip with [[thor|Þórr]] becomes the most famous of all the thunder-god's adventures.[^1]

The etymology is uncertain: the name is usually connected with Old Norse *hum* ‘darkness, dusk’, whence the traditional gloss ‘dark one’. The poem makes him Týr's father — a filiation the corpus elsewhere contradicts, since Snorri counts [[tyr|Týr]] among Óðinn's sons — and gives him the Edda's fullest portrait of a giant household: a loathsome nine-hundred-headed grandmother, a golden-browed mother who hides the guests under the great kettle, three oxen for supper, and a crystal cup no pillar can crack.[^1][^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Hymir** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in this name. The mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2: the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses, a statement about orthography and never about the figure. No domain is claimed: the plain-ASCII *hymir.com* is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.[^3]

sources.citation: Hymiskviða (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hymir, Týr.
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Hymir, hum.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Old Norse as **Hymir** (nominative; genitive *Hymis*). Its etymology is genuinely uncertain: the standard line, registered by Cleasby-Vigfusson and carried by Simek, connects it with Old Norse *hum* ‘darkness, dusk, twilight gloom’, yielding ‘dark one, dusky one’ — a fitting name for a frost-giant of the outer seas.[^1] The final *-r* is the Old Norse nominative ending. Because the name is pure ASCII, the fallback *hymir* loses nothing but the capital.

The name is not only a theonym-by-episode: the metrical þulur keep *Hymir* among the ordinary giant-heiti, the roster of names skaldic poets carried for the jötnar, which suggests the tradition treated him as a giant-type as much as a single character.[^2]

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **h** → **H** — Same, capitalized
- **y** → **y** — Same
- **m** → **m** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same

No domain is held for this name: the plain-ASCII *hymir.com* belongs to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release. The Unicode restoration **Hymir** is classified Tier 2 because it preserves nothing the ASCII form loses — the y the name carries is a letter ASCII shares with Old Norse.

sources.citation: Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Hymir, hum; Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hymir.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur of the jötnar, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈhy.mir/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **H-** — Voiceless glottal [h], fully sounded as in English *hill*
- **-y-** — Short close front rounded [y], the vowel of German *ü* or French *tu*: round the lips as for ‘oo’ while the tongue says ‘ee’; one of the Old Norse sounds English later unrounded and lost
- **-mir** — Voiced bilabial nasal [m], short [i], and the final nominative trill [r], lightly sounded after the vowel

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘HÜ-mir’ — stress on the first syllable, as in every Old Norse word, and the final r kept light.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Hymir, the giant of Hymiskviða and Gylfaginning
- **The þulur** — Hymir, carried as an ordinary giant-heiti in the skaldic name-lists
- **Skaldic tradition** — the unnamed giant of Bragi's *Ragnarsdrápa* (9th c.), Þórr's companion in the fishing-boat, conventionally identified as Hymir[^2]
- **Modern Icelandic** — Hymir, unchanged in spelling

Hymir is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing ASCII loses: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no marked vowel length. The tier is a report on the name's orthography, not a judgment on the giant's standing in the mythology.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology.
Bragi Boddason, Ragnarsdrápa, stanzas preserved in Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes (1987); cf. Lindow, Norse Mythology (2001), s.v. Hymir.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Hymir** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda, recording a poem whose matter the ninth-century shield-poetry shows to be centuries older.[^1] Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the younger futhark; no runic attestation of this name survives, so the manuscript form is the primary witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is a simplex, usually connected with Old Norse *hum* ‘darkness, dusk’, with the nominative singular ending *-r*.
- In the Younger Futhark it would have been carved ᚼᚢᛘᛁᛦ (h-u-m-i-R): the ᚢ rune covers the rounded vowel y, and ᛦ writes the final nominative -r.[^2]
- The y is the close front rounded vowel /y/ — Old Norse marks it with a distinct letter, and ASCII happens to share it, so nothing is lost in transit.
- The Unicode restoration Hymir is therefore identical to the input but for the capital; the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, and the record stays honest about it: no domain form of the name is held in the collection.

sources.citation: The Poetic Edda, trans. Larrington (2014), introduction to Hymiskviða; Bragi, Ragnarsdrápa, in Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957), runes and phonology.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Hymir** is catalogued under Giant, Owner of Cauldron — and the sources earn both terms: he is the Edda's most fully drawn giant householder, and his cauldron is the poem's whole cause.[^1]

### The Giant

Hymir is the jötunn at the eastern edge of heaven, east of the Élivágar: fierce, shrewd, often cruel to guests, descended from a nine-hundred-headed ancestress — yet a working householder with a byre, a boat, and fishing-grounds he rows to himself.

### The Sea

His domain is the cold outer water where the serpent lies: he pulls up two whales at once, and it is on his fishing-ground that [[thor|Þórr]] hooks the [[jormungandr|Miðgarðsormr]].

### The Cauldron

The roomy, hard-forged kettle ‘a mile deep’ is the only vessel in the world large enough to brew for all the Æsir — which is why the gods must come for it, and why the giant counts its loss beside the cup's.

### Hospitality and Its Price

The poem's real subject: the host who slaughters three oxen for his guests and tallies every mouthful, who frames the wagers himself and loses both the cup and the cauldron on them.

sources.citation: Hymiskviða (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014); Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 48, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography of Hymir is narrative rather than cultic — the corpus gives him no regalia, but the cauldron-quest fixed a small set of objects no retelling can omit:[^1]

- **The mile-deep cauldron** — the roomy kettle Týr names as his father's: the vessel of plenty kept in the giant-house until the gods carry it off on Þórr's head, its rim ringing at his heels
- **The ox-head bait** — the head of the black bull Himinbrjótr (Snorri's Himinhrjóðr), torn off for the fishing: the herd's finest traded for the serpent that girdles the world
- **The crystal cup** — the treasure no pillar could crack, shattered at last on the one harder thing in the hall: the giant's own skull, at the whispered counsel of Týr's golden-browed mother
- **The nine-hundred-headed grandmother** — the monstrous ancestry of the house, set in the poem's first stanzas against the fair counsellor who hides the guests
- **The two whales** — Hymir's own catch, hauled up at once on his hooks: the measure of the giant's strength, dwarfed by what rose to the ox-head
- **The lame goat** — one of Þórr's team lamed on the road home, which the poem lays at [[loki|Loki]]'s door: the quest's small lasting scar

sources.citation: Hymiskviða (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014); Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 48, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Hymir's mythology is a single great poem and its prose retelling: *Hymiskviða*, the lay of the cauldron-quest, and Gylfaginning 48, where Snorri gives the fishing-trip its sea-cold detail.[^1][^2]

### The Demand for the Cauldron (Hymiskviða 1–13)

The Æsir had hunted and taken auguries from the blood, and saw that [[aegir|Ægir]] — called also Gymir — had brew-stuff in plenty. Þórr ordered him to brew ale for the gods; Ægir, to be rid of the demand, set an impossible price: first let them bring a cauldron a mile wide. Týr knew where one stood: east of the Élivágar, at heaven's end, lives the shrewd Hymir — and ‘my fierce father owns the roomy kettle, a mile deep’. Þórr and Týr drove to the hall, met the loathsome nine-hundred-headed grandmother and the golden-browed mother, and were hidden under the great cauldron, for Hymir was often cruel to guests.[^1]

### The Host Comes Home (Hymiskviða 13–16)

Hymir came in from the hunting with the ice rattling in his beard; the pillar his gaze fell on burst apart, eight cauldrons crashed from the broken beam, and one hard-forged kettle came down whole. The hall fed the guests: three oxen were slaughtered, and Þórr alone ate two before he slept. In the morning the giant eyed his thinned herd and told his guest they must fish for the next day's meal.[^1]

### The Fishing for the Serpent (Hymiskviða 17–27; Gylfaginning 48)

Asked for bait, Þórr wrenched the head from the black bull Himinbrjótr. Hymir rowed hard, then harder, past his own grounds into water he called unsafe, where the serpent lies; he pulled up two whales at once, while Þórr cast the ox-head overboard. The Miðgarðsormr gaped on the bait, the hook caught, and Þórr braced his feet through the bottom of the boat and hauled the serpent's head to the gunwale — the two glaring, the boat nearly swamped — until the hammer struck and the serpent sank back into the sea. Hymir rowed home in gloomy silence.[^1][^2]

### The Cup, the Skull, and the Carrying-Off (Hymiskviða 28–39)

On land Hymir set the proof of strength: break his crystal cup. Twice Þórr hurled it through the stone pillars and twice it came back unbroken — until the fair counsellor whispered to strike it on Hymir's own skull, harder than any cup. The cup shattered, and Hymir mourned it: he could no longer say over it ‘ale is brewed’. Then he yielded the wager — take the cauldron, if you can carry it out. Týr heaved twice and could not shift it; Þórr hoisted it over his head and strode off with the rim ringing at his heels. Looking back, he saw Hymir coming from the caves with a troop of many-headed giants, set down the cauldron, and slew the whole host with Mjöllnir. One of Þórr's goats went lame on the road — Loki's doing, the poem says — but the cauldron came to Ægir, who brews in it for the Æsir ever after.[^1][^2]

### Elsewhere in the Corpus

Beyond the lay, Hymir lives in the name-lists and the shield: the þulur keep him among the giant-heiti, and Bragi's ninth-century *Ragnarsdrápa* paints the fishing-scene — the ox-head bait, the hooked serpent, the terrified giant at the gunwale — centuries before the manuscripts.[^3] Within the corpus his closest relations are [[aegir|Ægir]], whose feast demands the cauldron, [[tyr|Týr]], whom the poem makes his son, and [[thor|Þórr]], the guest his hall could not digest.

sources.citation: Hymiskviða (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 48, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Bragi Boddason, Ragnarsdrápa (stanzas in Skáldskaparmál); Skáldskaparmál þulur, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Hymir's poem has drawn comparatists for a century because the cauldron-quest is one of the old travelling stories of the North Atlantic: a vessel of plenty, kept by a grudging power beyond the sea, won for the feast of the gods. Scholars since Dumézil have set *Hymiskviða* beside the Celtic cauldron-quests — the Welsh *Preiddeu Annwfn*, where Arthur sails for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and the Irish cauldrons that no company leaves unsatisfied — and beside the Indo-European complex of the winning of the gods' drink.[^1]

The fishing scene travels its own trail: the thunder-god's combat with the sea-serpent belongs with the wide dragon-fight pattern, and the Norse corpus itself repeats the expedition with a different host — in Þórsdrápa the giant is [[geirrodr|Geirröðr]], and the primordial deep the serpent haunts is the one the gods built from [[ymir|Ymir]]'s body. Inside the corpus the neater tension is genealogical: *Hymiskviða* makes Hymir Týr's father, while Snorri elsewhere counts Týr among Óðinn's sons — two filiations the tradition never reconciled, and a standing exhibit in the study of how Eddic poems and Snorri's systematizing prose diverge.[^2]

sources.citation: Dumézil, Georges, Mythes et dieux des Germains: essai d'interprétation comparative (Paris: Leroux, 1939), on the cauldron-quest; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hymir.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Hall (D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hymir, Týr.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Hymir's afterlife is carried almost entirely by the fishing-trip, which became the most retold of all Þórr's adventures: the Kearys' *The Heroes of Asgard* (1857) and every handbook since keeps the ox-head, the glaring serpent, and the giant rowing home in silence.[^1]

In scholarship the poem holds a double distinction: it is the fullest portrait of a giant household in the Edda — the grandmother, the golden-browed mother, the counted oxen — and the standing northern exhibit in the comparative study of the cauldron-quest.[^2] The name itself stayed where the þulur put it: a giant-name, rarely borrowed, surfacing in modern fantasy and games chiefly as the surly host of the world's most famous fishing story.

sources.citation: Keary, Annie, and Eliza Keary, The Heroes of Asgard: Tales from Scandinavian Mythology (London: Macmillan, 1857); Orchard, Andy, Cassell's Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Hymir.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hymir, Hymiskviða.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Hymir is a textual figure: his attestations are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), which alone preserves *Hymiskviða*, and the manuscripts of Snorri's Edda; the þulur keep his name among the giant-heiti.[^1] The myth's antiquity, however, is proven by verse and stone. Bragi Boddason's *Ragnarsdrápa* (9th c.), composed for a painted shield, describes the fishing-scene — the ox-head bait, the hooked serpent, the hammer raised — with the giant aboard conventionally identified as Hymir: the story is centuries older than its manuscripts.[^2]

The picture-record follows. The Altuna runestone (U 1161, Uppland) shows the angler with his foot braced through the boat's bottom and the serpent on the line; the Gosforth Cross fishing-panel in Cumbria shows two figures in the boat — the angler and his giant companion.[^3] No cult site, toponym, or inscription names Hymir himself: he belongs to the world of poetry and the pictures poetry kept alive.

sources.citation: The Poetic Edda, trans. Larrington (2014), introduction to Hymiskviða.
Bragi Boddason, Ragnarsdrápa, stanzas preserved in Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Thor; Orchard, Cassell's Dictionary (1997), s.v. Hymir.

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
*Hymiskviða* — ‘The Lay of Hymir’ — is one of the Codex Regius's great comic-heroic lays and the giant's entire poetic dossier. Its construction is unusually full: a frame at Ægir's hall that sets the price of the feast; the road-east with Týr's tip about his father's kettle; the giant-household sketched in two women (the nine-hundred-headed grandmother, the golden-browed mother); the homecoming that shatters a pillar and eight cauldrons; the ox-feast; the rowing duel and the fishing for the Miðgarðsormr; the cup broken on the giant's skull; and the carrying-off of the cauldron under pursuit.[^1]

The poem's texture deserves note: it is thick with dialogue, wager-formulas, and household detail — the iced beard, the rattling pillars, the cauldron-rim ringing at Þórr's heels — and it weaves in other traditions at the edges, from Loki's laming of the goat to Ægir's by-name Gymir. Within the Edda it stands as the fullest account of Þórr's dealings with the giant-world and the principal source for the serpent-fishing alongside the skaldic shield-poems.[^2]

sources.citation: Hymiskviða (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
The Poetic Edda, trans. Larrington (2014), introduction to Hymiskviða; cf. Lindow, Norse Mythology (2001), s.v. Hymiskviða.

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
Gylfaginning 48 is Snorri's retelling of the cauldron-quest, and it both follows the poem and rearranges it. Snorri keeps the frame — Þórr's demand that Ægir brew, the impossible price of a cauldron a mile wide, Týr's knowledge of his father's kettle — and the great scenes: the two oxen eaten at supper, the ox-head bait (Snorri names the bull Himinhrjóðr), the rowing contest, the serpent at the gunwale, the cup broken on Hymir's skull at the woman's whisper, the cauldron carried off with its rim at Þórr's heels, the slaughter of the pursuing giants, and the lame goat.[^1]

Snorri's own additions are characteristic: he has Þórr carry the boat and the whales up from the shore as a further feat, and he closes by sending the cauldron to Ægir, who now brews ale in it each winter — a deliberate stitch to the *Lokasenna*, the feast at which Loki's flyting unfolds. Elsewhere the Prose Edda keeps Hymir in its systematic lists: Skáldskaparmál's þulur count his name among the jötnar, and the shield-stanzas of Bragi's *Ragnarsdrápa* that Snorri quotes in Skáldskaparmál preserve the fishing-scene from the ninth century.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 48, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (Ragnarsdrápa; þulur of the jötnar), trans. Faulkes (1987, 1998).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
No runic inscription names the giant Hymir: no stone invokes him, no carving carries his name, and the name does not circulate in the anthroponymy the way the gods' name-elements do.[^1]

What the runic and carved record does preserve is his myth. The Altuna runestone (U 1161, Uppland, Sweden) frames its inscription around a picture of the serpent-fishing: the angler in the boat, one foot thrust through the bottom boards as the poem describes, the line running down to the coiled serpent. The scene is the standing proof that *Hymiskviða*'s set-piece circulated in carving as well as verse in the Viking Age — though the stone names the rune-carver's dead, not the giant.[^2] Across the sea, the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria carves the fishing-panel with two figures in the boat: the angler and his giant companion.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hymir.
Orchard, Andy, Cassell's Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (Cassell, 1997), s.v. Hymir, on the Altuna and Gosforth scenes.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond the Eddas, Hymir's medieval afterlife runs through the skaldic tradition rather than the saga prose. The oldest witness is Bragi Boddason's *Ragnarsdrápa* (9th c.), the shield-poem whose surviving stanzas — quoted by Snorri in Skáldskaparmál — paint the fishing-expedition: the ox-head going overboard, the serpent gulping the bait, the giant aboard shrinking in terror. The giant is unnamed in the surviving verses, but the standard scholarly identification is Hymir, which would make the poem older than any manuscript of the myth by four centuries.[^1]

The pattern the poem fixes — Þórr as guest in a giant's hall, tested at table, at sea, and in feats of strength — is the one the corpus repeats with other hosts: with [[geirrodr|Geirröðr]] in Þórsdrápa and its prose retelling, where there is no hospitality at all, and in the broader cycle of Þórr's journeys east. Saxo's *Gesta Danorum*, which euhemerizes so much of the mythology, knows the thunderer's giant-contests without preserving the Hymir episode as such — a reminder that *Hymiskviða* and Snorri are the story's two real homes.[^2]

sources.citation: Bragi Boddason, Ragnarsdrápa, stanzas in Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes (1987); cf. Lindow, Norse Mythology (2001), s.v. Hymir.
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979); Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology (1993), s.v. Hymir.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Hymir is the Edda's portrait of hospitality under strain: the host who slaughters two oxen for his guest and counts the cost, who rows farther than he means to because pride will not let him ship his oar first, who frames both wagers himself — the cup, the cauldron — and loses both.[^1]

The poem never makes him a monster. It gives him a monstrous ancestry and a working farm, a mother who counsels against him and a treasure he genuinely mourns, and lets the comedy and the cold do the work. What the story measures is not his failure but the difference between keeping plenty and sharing it: the cauldron that now brews for all the gods spent its best years in a hall where even a guest's supper was tallied.
